chicken-breast-baked-or-broiled-skin-eat.title: Chicken breast, baked or broiled, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut taken from the pectoral muscle of the bird. When baked or broiled with the skin left on, it offers a juicy texture, mild flavor, and moderate fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast is the most ordered chicken cut in fast‑food and restaurant menus.
The skin adds roughly 30 % of the total calories but also provides beneficial fatty acids and vitamin E.
Baking at 180 °C retains up to 90 % of the original protein content.
Poultry meat is rich in cis‑linoleic acid, considered heart‑healthy.
In the United States, over 70 % of chicken consumption is breast meat.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving delivers about 31 g of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken breast contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immunity, and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low fat when skin removed
items.content: Skin‑less breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Salmonella contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: High sodium in restaurant versions
items.content: Fast‑food preparations often add salt and sauces, raising sodium levels.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Eating the skin increases calories and saturated fat, which may be undesirable for heart‑health concerns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, sliced in salads, sandwiches, wraps, or as chunks in rice and pasta dishes. The skin can be left on for extra flavor and crispness, or removed to reduce calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for 2‑3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Cress (Lepidium sativum) is an annual herb commonly used as a fresh garnish. When cooked, the leaves retain a mild peppery flavor, become tender, and are suitable for soups, side dishes, and fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cress belongs to the Brassicaceae family and is closely related to radish and mustard.
Its seeds germinate within 2–3 days, making it a popular indoor micro‑green.
Historically, cress was used as a medicinal herb for colds and digestive troubles.
Cress is rich in vitamin C, which degrades quickly during storage, so freshness matters.
In Japan, cooked cress is often served as a puree with soy sauce.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked cress retains a notable amount of vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in cress help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The fiber content promotes healthy bowel movements and may relieve constipation.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A serving of cooked cress provides very few calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Cress supplies potassium, calcium, and iron, essential for electrolyte balance and blood health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cress, manifested as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If grown conventionally, pesticide residues may remain on the leaves; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Cress contains modest levels of oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked cress can be added to soups, stews, vegetable casseroles, or used as a filling for crepes and dumplings. It also works well pureed with olive oil and lemon juice as a sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cress in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Pike (Esox lucius) is a predatory freshwater fish found in rivers, lakes and ponds across the Northern Hemisphere. Its firm, white flesh has a mild flavor and is commonly used in traditional Eastern European dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pike can accelerate quickly, reaching speeds up to 10 m/s.
It has two rows of sharp teeth that can protrude when the mouth opens.
Pike may live more than 15 years in the wild.
In Russia, pike is a symbol of strength and agility and appears in many folk tales.
Pike meat is high in protein and low in calories, making it popular among dietitians.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pike provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The fish contains very little saturated fat, suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pike offers phosphorus, selenium and potassium, which support bone health and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Although lower than in oily fish, pike still provides EPA and DHA.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked pike may contain parasites, so thorough cooking is recommended.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: As a top predator, pike can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pike.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pike is often pan‑fried, baked, steamed, or used in fish soups. Fillets are commonly marinated in lemon juice before cooking to soften the firm texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pike in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Martini is a renowned brand of dry vermouth created in Italy in 1863. The drink is made from white wine, aromatic herbs and spices, and is often used as a base for cocktails.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Martini was created in the town of Pombretto (Turin) in 1863.
There are several Martini variants: Dry, Sweet (Rosso), White (Bianco) and flavored (e.g., Martini Rosato).
Martini is closely associated with the classic “Martini” cocktail, traditionally served in a cocktail glass with an olive or a lemon twist.
The brand has used famous ambassadors, including James Bond, who preferred his Martini “shaken, not stirred.”

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Herbal infusions used in vermouth are rich in polyphenols, which may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate consumption can promote relaxation
items.content: Alcohol in small amounts has a calming effect, helping to reduce stress.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Martini contains alcohol, so it should be consumed responsibly and avoided during pregnancy, driving, or when contraindicated.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet variants (Rosso, Bianco) may contain significant sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to the herbal extracts used in the formulation.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve Martini chilled in a cocktail glass, often with an olive, lemon twist, or cocktail cherry. It is used as the base for classic cocktails such as the Martini, Manhattan, Negroni, and others.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the Martini bottle in a cool, dark place with the cap tightly sealed. After opening, it is best consumed within 6–12 months to preserve its aromatic qualities.
